 The Lies We Tell About Poverty and Welfare
 Americans are told to be proud of sacrifice and self-reliance. That story didn’t come from nowhere — and it comes at a steep cost.

 Every society runs on stories it mistakes for facts. In America, those stories shape who gets help, who gets blamed, and who is left out. Not My Narrative is a Next City series that debunks the pervasive myths that have been used to justify neglect, inequity, and the status quo — and elevates the people proving those myths wrong. 
 This week, in “ Making Ends Meet vs There’s Plenty to Go Around,” we’re talking about how society has made stretching oneself thin a point of pride. Check out the podcast on Apple and Spotify . 
 As the United States marked the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence this year, talk of the so-called American Dream has been everywhere. The tenets of the American Dream originate from that same declaration, as well as the Preamble to the Constitution, both of which promise to ensure that every person in the nation will have the freedom and opportunities needed to prosper. 
 But over time, that ideal has morphed into something a lot less hopeful — the idea that one must prosper on one’s own without the help of others, even when that means stretching resources and tightening belts at the cost of one’s health, happiness, or time with loved ones. “The reason we have a narrative that you’ve got to make ends meet on your own is because of that American Dream story,” says Tom Mould, a professor at Rollins College and author of Overthrowing the Queen: Telling Stories of Welfare in America (affiliate link).
 Overthrowing the Queen:
Telling Stories of Welfare in America 
 But the idea that every person is set up to succeed if only they sacrifice and demonstrate enough grit and determination ignores structural problems and stigmatizes those who seek and receive needed support. “If you’ve got this narrative that says that to be moral and to be American is to work hard and be independent, then you’re going to feel embarrassed and ashamed if you can’t live up to that American ideal,” Mould explains. On a societal level, this can translate into blaming low-income people for their own financial hardships and designing support programs that punish and ostracize rather than just provide help. 
 But research consistently shows that the conditions that produce financial hardships are systemic. Entrenched racism , sexism, and other structural inequalities prevent many members of marginalized groups from achieving even basic financial security .
 The country’s economic system is also stacked against working people. As of January 2026, the nation’s 12 richest billionaires had a collective net worth of over $2.7 trillion. Meanwhile, minimum wage has yet to crest $10.00 per hour in states like North Dakota, Idaho, and much of the U.S. South. According to an Institute for Policy Studies analysis , even as the nation’s richest residents have accumulated more wealth, they have paid a smaller share of total U.S. taxes. That analysis found that in 2018, the tax share of the top 0.01% of Americans was close to what it had been in 1953. But their share of the nation’s wealth had nearly quadrupled during the same period.
 Rather than confront those realities, members of the press, lawmakers, and other public figures often spread harmful stereotypes to obscure them. Perhaps none is better known than the racist stereotype of the welfare queen, which was popularized during the Reagan era and is most often used to disparage Black women and other women of color. “If you plot out the welfare queen story, it is point for point the opposite of the American Dream,” Mould says. “The welfare queen story says instead of hard work, there’s no work; instead of independence, there’s dependence; instead of a family of four, there’s a single mother with multiple kids from different parents.” 
 While Ronald Reagan spread a caricature of supposed promiscuous and idle welfare queens defrauding the government and hard-working taxpayers while on the campaign trail and in the White House beginning in the 1970s, the origin of the stereotype goes back further. For example, when sociologists Kenneth Neubeck and Noël Cazenave examined historical sources for their book, Welfare Racism: Playing the Race Card Against America’s Poor (affiliate link), they found that Black mothers were often denied pensions from the U.S. Children’s Bureau during the Progressive Era because of beliefs that they “have always gotten along,” and that if they were given pensions “all they’ll do is have more children.”
 Even relative champions of the welfare state have fed into these destructive narratives. Franklin D. Roosevelt, in a Depression-era address, once referred to government support for unemployed workers as “a narcotic, a subtle destroyer of the human spirit” and “in violation of the traditions of America.” Mould says the speech is an example of how “the idea that generational poverty is unacceptable [and] that this is somehow not outside of these people’s control gets conveyed at the top levels of power.”
 The pernicious cultural ideal that one ought to make ends meet on one’s own without outside support is often traced to the strong influence of Protestant, and particularly Calvinist, theology on American cultural mores. Those religious traditions emerged in 16th-century Europe, and their adherents were the first to settle in what would later become the United States. They are known for promoting principles of thrift, discipline, hard work, and individualism. But some scholars have contested the historical narrative that draws a line from Protestant settlers to today’s hustle culture. Revolutionary-era Americans, they argue, held a more communal vision of human flourishing — one that looks quite different from the rugged individualism we now treat as tradition. 
 Still, there is no doubt that aspects of the so-called Protestant work ethic are held up as ideals in America today. That term was coined by sociologist Max Weber in his book The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (affiliate link), which was first published in German in 1905 and later translated into English in 1930. Weber argued that Protestant ethics and values drove the spread of modern capitalism, though he noted that the spiritual underpinnings of calls to work hard and be frugal had all but disappeared by the early 20th century. Whereas “the Puritan wanted to work in calling,” Weber wrote that the modern worker was “bound to the technical and economic conditions of machine production.”
 Another piece of the colonial American past more directly shaped how the United States has built its welfare infrastructure: the Elizabethan Poor Law Act of 1601 . Colonists used that English legislation as a guide for developing government-run poor relief programs in early America. The law drew a harsh line between those who were deemed “worthy” or “unworthy” of help, sorting people into three categories: able-bodied, children, and the “impotent,” a label used for aging and disabled people.
 By the late 19th century, those distinctions had found new justification in social Darwinism , a pseudoscientific field that linked the biological concept of natural selection to economic success. The field emerged in the latter half of the 19th century and grew more popular from there, fueling early versions of racialized stereotypes like the welfare queen.
 During America’s Gilded Age, in the last decades of the 19th century, social Darwinism was also used to explain the rise of titans such as John D. Rockefeller and Andrew Carnegie. The idea that these men possessed inherent characteristics that destined them for success in the corporate world was a convenient justification for the incredible wealth they amassed while the nation’s poor grew poorer, urban slums sprawled, and public health crises raged. “The growth of a large business is merely a survival of the fittest ,” Rockefeller once claimed. Today, Rockefeller, Carnegie, and other business giants of their era are still held up as models of the American Dream.
 Though social Darwinism largely fell out of fashion during the 20th century as scientific research undermined its claims and studies in the humanities laid bare its harmful effects on societies, the modern conservative movement in the United States has embraced the school of thought once again. It uses social Darwinism’s disproven pseudoscientific ideas to rationalize policies like rolling back social support programs and cutting taxes for the rich — policies that threaten to worsen inequalities and push working-class families over the edge.
 “The problem is this stigma is not just about making somebody feel bad — it actually has a really big economic impact,” says Mould. This is true both in the way that the stigma shapes government policies and in how it shapes the circumstances of people who need support. 
 A cart of food is delivered to the Senate chamber on June 30, 2025 as Republicans begin a final push to advance President Donald Trump's tax breaks and spending cuts package, at the Capitol in Washington. (Mark Schiefelbein / AP)
 Just look to the Trump administration’s new Medicaid work requirements . The new rules are expected to strip coverage from thousands of parents and childless adults who do not have income equal to 80 hours of work at the federal minimum wage, as well as disabled people and cancer patients who have historically been exempted from such requirements. 
 Already, some states have work and behavior requirements that prevent some from accessing Transitional Assistance for Needy Families. Among the requirements that some states enforce are drug testing, the denial of benefits to those convicted of a drug felony, and the refusal to increase benefits for families who have another child while enrolled in the program.
 A person in need of support must not only overcome the friction of such requirements, but also the stigma — both social and internalized — that comes with being raised among these persistent narratives of noble self-reliance and the promise of American prosperity. 
 One study of more than 2,000 mothers receiving public benefits across 15 states found that more than 60% reported experiencing stigma; over half reported internalizing stigma. The study also found a significant link between welfare stigma and a mother rating her health as bad or very bad.
 “That dominant culture tells us to be independent,” says Jeremy Goshorn, a professor at Lebanon Valley College and a practicing mental health counselor. Because of that, Goshorn says, “asking for help can feel like failure. It can impact components of an individual’s self-esteem, how they view themselves, [and contribute to] self-deprecating and self-defeating thought processes.” 
 But he and Mould say that another world is possible. While we do the long-term work of organizing movements to tear down the structural barriers that prevent families and communities from prospering, there are personal changes we can make to disrupt these entrenched narratives. 
 “We have to tell better stories,” says Mould. To do that, he recommends choosing stories based on the values and perspective of the listener, asking the listener to think of a time when they have experienced a similar hardship, and keeping things simple. The simplicity of narratives like the Reagan-era welfare queen is a large part of what has made them stick, despite their distance from reality. 
 Goshorn says it is also vital to examine our own biases around giving and receiving help. Why do we tend to distrust a neighbor who asks for help covering their rent, but admire startup founders who burn through investor money? Why do we fund programs that require sobriety before receiving housing and call that compassion? 
 Unlearning instincts like these is a first step to building community. Goshorn says: “It moves us out of our individualistic way of being into a more collaborative community way of being.”
